Desert cloth is created with a loom and is primarily used for power level 7 armour.

(Journal)
You might think that any cloth found in the desert could be called desert cloth, but you’d just be arguing semantics and that won’t win you many friends at parties. No, the desert cloth we refer to here is the sort of thing woven from desert weed and cacti fibres. It is forged of the desert, not simply found within it.

More elegant and refined than cotton cloth, this fabric was very popular among Emberwood citizenry. They would craft beautiful dresses, fine shirts and elegant robes, many of which included patterns of undulating blue and black in honour of the serpentine dances they would watch in the sky, as Imaru and Xikotal swam the air currents together.

detail.description:
Infinity cloth is created with a loom and is primarily used for power level 7 armour.

(Journal)
Some fabrics are too beautiful for mundane hands. It feels almost a crime that you, a mere mortal, should be allowed to hold such a material. To craft it into clothing is an act so sacred, that priests should be set up solely to handle this fabric.

At least that’s what some tailors believe.

Infinity cloth is so garish, so incoherently vibrant, that it induces a strange sort of psychosis into those who use it. They do not see the vulgar brightness of the colours, nor the incomprehensible combinations that would be a fashion crime in any other world. Instead, they see only shimmering colours and a sparkling iridescence that reaches somewhere inside of them and murders their sense of taste.

Infinity cloth is a beautiful blasphemy, handle with care.

detail.description:
Mystic cloth is a item used for armours. It is crafted at the loom using three mystic thread.

(Journal)
It is almost imperceptible, but mystic cloth hums. It's the magical resonance: the elemental threads pushing against each other as their charge shifts. That oscillation also means that there is a lightly massaging effect on the wearer. It's entirely possible to feel calm from the vibrations as you stride into battle.

You might also be misstaken for thinking that mystic cloth is blue. On a microscopic level, it's actually a multitude of colours, combining to form the illusion of blue. As a magician once told me, it's the same effect as a blue sky: it is the result of all the colours in the world combining to make a wondrous azure.

Vis Cloth is a processed material created at a Loom and is primarily used for power level 8 armour.

(Journal)
Vis cloth is not the most comfortable material to wear. It's waxy, leaving a thin magical residue on the skin when worn. Wizards have compared it to skinning and wearing a giant slug, which isn't the best of adverts. They have complained about peeling it from their skin after a day of magical combat. If you're a hirsute magical user, you should be warned that it can rip a layer of hair from you whenever you use it. The wizards of Ashenfall's past may have had long beards, but you can be sure that there wasn't a scrap of hair on the rest of their bodies.

A discerning archer would do well to craft blue dragonhide leather. The colour is fetching, the defence against magic is second-to-none, and the material has an elasticity that makes it perfect for the nimble stuff that archers tend to do.

If it has a downside, it's a little tight. There's no hiding in blue dragonhide chaps, for example: all the lumps and bumps are out there.

(Journal)
You may wonder where the "cursed" moniker comes from. There is no need to worry. You're not cursed by wearing it, nor will making it mean you'll be visited by the three dragons of past, present and future in the night. It has a wildly different etymology.

The "cursed" is a tannery thing, you see. Cursed leather is notoriously hard to work and shape. Only the foremost tanners can manipulate it. But even they have a hard time, often exclaiming "cursed leather!" at the top of their lungs

detail.description:
Dire wolf leather can be created by tanning dire wolf hide at a tannery.

(Journal)
The tanned hide of a powerful dire wolf. It's sturdy, thick, ready for enchantment and more resilient than normal leather. 

A legend speaks of a warrior that wore the tanned hide of a dire wolf. He wore it proudly as he walked the streets and used it to strike fear into the hearts of bandits and criminals alike. After all, a warrior that could best such a beast, was no one to be trifled with.

The story goes that one day he met another warrior, proud, skillful and handsome, and the two of them became the best of friends. They would fight together, spar together and rescued helpless villagers as an unstoppable pair. Until the night of the full moon, where the truth was revealed. Where once his new friend had stood, there was now a dread wolf of midnight-black fur and eyes of burning coal. They fought again, but gone was the jovial sparring of friends. Now they fought as man and beast, tooth and claw versus blade and shield, until all that was left of the two of them was this story.

(Journal)
Tanned hide infused with a dragon's vigour, draconic leather was a game-changing discovery to the people of Fellhollow. It was as flexible as normal leather, but more resilient than even the hardened skins, and it could be fashioned into many shapes for a variety of armored styles.

For a short while, the fashionistas of Emberwood village would use this leather to create garments that evoked the majesty of their draconic protectors, without bearing the scales that might cause undue offence.

(Journal)
Is it ingenuity or hubris to refine the mighty scales of a dragon down into this thick and sturdy leather?  To the Wild Knights it was the natural order. Hides became leather, which became a resilient second skin they would wear whilst riding into battle. Favoured by archers and scouts due to the nimble flexibility of the scales, yet still acting as a resilient bulwark against sword, arrow and claw alike.  To the people of Emberwood village, however, such sights were akin to blasphemy. Whilst the green dragons showed little mercy, the villagers loved and adored their majestic draconic protectors, Imaru and Xikotal, and they thought that wearing the skin of their kind might potentially cause offence.

detail.description:
Kalphite shell is a basic item used as a crafting material. It can be processed from kalphite shell fragments with acrid adhesive at the tannery.

(Journal)
Ah, very good: you have cottoned onto something that mainland Gielinor has failed to understand. The way to make armour as strong as a kalphite's exoskeleton is not to hammer it into shapes that are suitable for humans. The carapace is too resistant, and you will get an armour that is ill-fitting for the human form. There will be plenty of gaps for someone to slip a Keris into.

What you need to do is break the shell into its component fragments. You need to make a kind of kalphite mosaic, then adhere it with something acrid to make it into an armour. That's how you become as hardy as a kalphite.

(Journal)
There is no better advert for red dragon leather than Fuzan. The tyrant of Umbral Sands has seen his fair share of upstarts. Moon Garou of all shapes and sizes have confronted him over the years, and none have managed to break his red leather hide. The only blades to have cut him were the claws of his mother, and the glaive of one mutinous KotHaar. Fuzan has met very little resistance over his long life, which might go some way to explaining why he is the way he is.

Black Dragon Leather is a processed material created with one black dragon hide, one dragon blood and one ground rune essence in the advanced tannery that can be used to craft power level 8 equipment.

(Journal)
Rangers are stealthy little blighters. They like nothing more than to crouch behind a mushroom and ping arrows at a target, preferably without being seen. That preference makes black dragon leather hugely attractive to a ranger. Not only does it bend nicely at the joints for the mushroom-crouching, it's highly durable and - best of all - it's black, which makes the whole subterfuge thing more likely to succeed. I've always suspected that rangers like the black as it makes them look a bit edgy, but that's unproven.

Nothing has adapted to the Scorch better than the kalphite. Even the KotHaar have to take occasional precautions, returning to shade and cooling their bodies. But the reason you see so many kalphite in the desert is because they thrive in it, growing in numbers while goats, desert devils and other creatures can barely survive.

The human condition is, of course, to see something admirable and then kill it and wear it. Lo, we have Scorch Leather: kalphite, reduced to a potential hat.

(Journal)
There are many steps to making mystic robes - fibres to thread, thread to cloth, cloth to robes - but you would be wise not to skip any of them. Habberdash the Impatient, a magician who live in the Temple Woods, attempted to make his robes solely from thread. He would wrap himself, round and round, with spool after spool of mystic thread, and then attempt battle.  You can imagine how it went. He got snagged on a goblin's helmet and quickly unwound, mid-battle. We're not sure who would have been more shocked: Habberdash, who promptly got stabbed in the gut, or the goblin, who was confronted with a wizard in his undergarments.

(Journal)
Blue dragon dust is one of those things where you wonder who invented it, and what curious sequence of events led to it happening. Some unknown person had the wherewithal to strip a dragon of dragon scales, crush those scales in a pestle and mortar, then apply the resulting dust to a potion. Not only that, they downed said potion and stood in the path of a dragon. Does that not seem inexorably mad to you?

But thank you, inexorably mad person, because now we have this potent ingredient which can protect a person from dragonfire. You have been forgotten in time, but your blue dusty legacy lives on.

Alchemists and specialists in herbal remedies would be lying if they said they hadn't considered the medicinal properties of Kuldra. They imagine what it would be like if they could get hold of one of her teeth, crush it, and then use it in place of the traditional ground dragon tooth. Just how much of a kick would that give their concoctions? They're self-aware enough to know that it's just a fantasy, but they like to daydream about it anyway. Sure, it would be lovely to rid the world of a tyrant dragon, but think of the potions!

Do these scattered pieces of KotHaar consciousness communicate with each other on some level? Does a bag of ground obsidian contain more information than any library? We have SO many questions.

(Journal)
It's not advised to eat a rune whole. You can bet it's one of the first things that someone did when runes were discovered. In it pops. But the result is anticlimactic: runes don't release any magical properties while they're in there. Earth runes won't magically solve any gall stones; an astral rune won't bless your small-intestine as it worms its way southwards. Then there's the whole 'exiting' thing: passing a rune is not particularly pleasurable.

Crushing a rune beforehand, though? That's slightly more likely to create magical side-effects. Having control over those side-effects, however, is a whole other matter.

Congratulations on being midway through the making-tea process. Keep going: we believe in you. Soon, you will have a hot mug of tea in your hands, and nothing - not the ever-approaching prospect of facing Kuldra - will be able to intrude on your peace.

(Journal)
The walking dead are strange things, animated by hunger, need, rage and a touch of magic. In Ashenfall it is the hunger of Imaru that drives them, as her great maw draws in the souls of both the living and the dead, the afflicted try to cling to life with everything that they have.

They fail, but the drive remains. Fear, desperation, and simple need keeps the body moving, if not alive. This changes the body, that hunger and rot seeping into the very bones and changing them to be something other than they were.

When ground down, these bones become a powder containing hints of that animating magic. A necromantic resonance with a wide range of uses.

What's better than a dead tree? A dead tree that has been burned to the point of carbonization. No longer do you see unsightly green leaves, but now the wonderful blackness of charcoal. Highly praised by smiths. Way better than stupid old logs of wood.

This journal entry was sponsored by the tree haters of , if you're interested in joining their focus group, please speak to Tim near Bob's Axes.

It's almost impossible to hold dried tea leaves up to the nose, have a huff, and not go "aaaaaah" in a deep, relieved sort of manner. It's the smell of lazy Sunday afternoons, butt in a rocking chair, wistfully thinking back to your golden years.

A collection of pelt scraps collected from smaller creatures. Some druids would insist on crafting cloaks made only from smaller animals that died of natural causes. This meant that each cloak often took months, or sometimes even years, to craft. Naturally this wasn’t particularly helpful on the cusp of winter.
